1 
 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, LLC  
  
) 
) 
)  
   
                   
Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                         
 
SUPPORTIVE COMMENTS AND LIMITED PROTEST OF THE NEW JERSEY 
BOARD OF PUBLIC UTILITIES 
 
On August 13, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) proposed revisions to the 
Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) and the PJM Open 
Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”).1  
This proposed service would be implemented by PJM during periods of insufficient resources to 
reliably meet demand in real-time operations, enabling PJM to prioritize load reduction in 
zones/areas where New Large Loads have not brought their own new capacity or had their capacity 
needs covered through the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”).  The New Jersey Board of 
Public Utilities (“Board”) supports the Proposal with a limited protest, as it presents a largely 
workable solution to the region’s resource adequacy shortfall and appropriately incentivizes New 
Large Loads in the region to bring new capacity to the system.   
I. 
Background 
PJM is facing a period of unprecedented structural scarcity.  For the first time in history, 
PJM’s Base Residual Auction (“BRA”) for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year (“DY”) cleared short of 
 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large 
Load Registry to Address System Reliability, Docket No. ER26-3515 (Aug. 13, 2026) (“PJM IRAS 
Proposal” or “Proposal”).

2 
 
its Reliability Requirement by 6.6 gigawatts (“GW”), 2 and the BRA for the following 2028/2029 
DY followed suit, clearing 6.8 GW short of PJM’s Reliability Requirement.3  This shortfall is 
largely attributable to rapid load growth from data centers, as approximately 30 of the 32 GW of 
projected peak load growth between 2024 and 2030 is attributable to these customers.4  PJM stated 
that “[t]his onrush of demand has…raised future resource adequacy concerns.”5  This growth is 
forecasted to persist, with PJM predicting summer peak load increases of 65.7 GW over the next 
ten years and 96.7 GW over the next 20 years.6   
To confront this, PJM held a Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) Large Load Additions 
(“LLA”) workstream beginning in September 2025,7 and a main discussion point centered on 
differential reliability for certain new large load customers.  A PJM Board Decisional Letter 
concluded this workstream and directed PJM staff to develop the mechanics of this differential

auction procures-134479-mw-of-generation-resources.pdf [https://perma.cc/A89W-W99B]. 
3 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction Report, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 3 (July 14, 2026) (“PJM 
2028/2029 BRA Report”), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-
info/2028-2029/2028-2029-bra results-report.pdf [https://perma.cc/A53K-TXXY].

issuance of the August 2025 Board Letter, PJM has published its 2026 Long-Term Load Forecast Report.  
Forecasting improvements have resulted in the peak load forecast for 2030 to be revised downwards by

5 Ibid.

report tables.xlsx.

item-06---critical-issue-fast-path---large-load-additions---issue-charge.pdf.

3 
 
reliability service.  Specifically, it stated that new LLAs should be subject to curtailment prior to 
the deployment of pre-emergency Demand Response (“DR”) if they do not offset their growth 
with incremental generation.8  This initiated a separate stakeholder process to specifically focus 
on this differential reliability service, the Connect and Manage (“C&M”) Senior Task Force, which 
was eventually combined with PJM’s CIFP-RBP.  The stakeholder process for this CIFP concluded 
with a July 2026 PJM Board Decisional Letter requiring electric distribution companies (“EDC”) 
to implement a similar differential reliability service, though changed to “IRAS,” for new Large 
Loads that do not bring sufficient capacity.9   
Therefore, PJM’s Proposal at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) 
reflects almost a year of deliberation and stakeholder engagement surrounding the feasibility and 
potential implications of implementing such a program.  The Board thinks PJM’s Proposal presents 
thoughtful consideration of the various stakeholder proposals and perspectives and thinks its final 
IRAS plan strikes an appropriate balance between state and federal jurisdictional divisions in the 
Federal Power Act (“FPA”).  While there are certain elements of the Proposal that the Board does 
not support, these elements are not consequential to the foundational principles or procedures of 
IRAS and could be modified, or severed and rejected, without undermining the overall package 
reforms.10  In some instances, the Board is simply asking for additional clarification from PJM.  
Ultimately, the Board is appreciative of PJM’s leadership role to initiate and lead this mandatory 
 
8 Letter from David Mills, Interim President & CEO, PJM Bd. of Managers, to PJM Stakeholders 
(January 16, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-
disclosures/2026/20260116-pjm-board-letter-re-results-of-the-cifp-process-large-load-additions.pdf.  
9 PJM Bd. of Managers, Board Decisional Letter on Critical Issue Fast Path – Reliability Backstop 
Procurement and Connect and Manage (July 27, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-
pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2026/20260727-board-decisional-letter-on-cifp-reliability-backstop-
procurement-and-connect-and-manage.pdf. 
10 PJM IRAS Proposal at 9-10 (consenting to FERC’s modification and severance of individual elements 
of the proposed Tariff and RAA language).

4 
 
PJM-led curtailment service and Large Load Registry and thinks it falls squarely within PJM’s 
authority in maintaining resource adequacy at the wholesale level.  The Board also appreciates that 
PJM is proposing to exclude New Large Loads from future capacity market demand curves if they 
do not bring their own new capacity onto the system.  This treatment will help protect ratepayers 
from capacity market cost increases that would have been caused by future large loads. 
IRAS is an important step to protect the PJM system, but it is only one step of many.  
Crucially, PJM has workstreams to address the supply-and-demand imbalance alongside IRAS.  
These include the RBP, the Expedited Interconnection Track, and the Reliability Resource 
Initiative, which primarily focus on getting new megawatts (“MW”) of supply online.  However, 
it will likely take many years for this new supply to start contributing energy to the grid, with 
project development timelines extended due to supply chain constraints and siting and permitting 
delays.  Therefore, IRAS serves as an important operational resource adequacy tool for PJM.  The 
work is not over, however.  More reforms at the PJM and state levels will be needed to bring 
stability to prices and reliability.  
II. 
Interim Resource Adequacy Service 
The Board appreciates PJM’s decision to propose a PJM-led resource adequacy service for 
New Large Loads that fail to offset their registered peak load with sufficient capacity arrangements 
through Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) or by being allocated a share of the RBP 
Unforced Capacity (“UCAP”) MW.  PJM’s Proposal is a departure from PJM staff’s Stage 4 CIFP 
RBP/C&M proposal, which envisioned a voluntary state-led program,11 and the Board appreciates 
PJM’s tenacity in advancing a PJM-led program instead.  The PJM-led approach addresses the 
 
11 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., “PJM Connect & Manage CIFP Proposal Stage 4” (June 23, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-rbp/2026/20260630/20260630-item-02a--
-pjm-stage-4-proposal---connect-and-manage---executive-summary.pdf.

5 
 
collective action problem and ensures that ratepayers across the region can be protected, even if 
their states and other states pursue different policies for large load developments. 
At a high level, this new service will enable the grid operator to direct load shed directives 
to each zone/area during grid stress events in an amount commensurate with its uncovered New 
Large Load capacity.  In other words, PJM is directing a differential reliability service to those 
who have contributed the most to the grid’s current resource adequacy shortfall, New Large Load 
customers.  This tool will help PJM maintain reliability for the system when the grid is short of 
capacity, specifically helping maintain reliability for existing customers.  Importantly, this 
proposed step will be initiated prior to calling on Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions 
Actions,12 which will help maintain the participation of certain load management reduction 
resources, like DR, by minimizing “fatigue” that can occur from being over-called on during stress 
events.   
The Board thinks the placement for IRAS in PJM’s Emergency Procedures framework 
creates a strong incentive for New Large Loads to engage in bilateral agreements, which is the best 
way to protect ratepayers from the costs and risks associated with load growth from these 
customers while also resulting in new MW of supply to the system.  In sum, the Board thinks this 
Proposal: (1) takes a strong initiative to confront the resource adequacy shortfall facing the system 
at large; (2) provides teeth to incentivize New Large Loads to contribute new capacity to the grid; 
(3) respects the state and federal jurisdictional division outlined in the FPA; and (4) avoids the 
collective action problem of PJM’s previous state opt-in proposal.  The Board will work with 
relevant state entities, utilities, large loads, and PJM to ensure that the IRAS quantity aligns with 
 
12 PJM IRAS Proposal, Attachments A and B, at Attachment DD-4, section I(b).

6 
 
Eligible New Large Loads in New Jersey’s zones, and to ensure that appropriate policies and 
protocols are in place to direct IRAS to these Eligible New Large Loads by June 1, 2027.  
 
Limited Protest - Already-Cleared Resources Should Not Qualify for BYONC 
While the Board generally supports the BYONC criteria that PJM lists in Attachment DD-
4 section VI,13 the Board is not supportive of PJM’s decision to include capacity that cleared in the 
BRAs for the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 DYs to qualify as BYONC-eligible resources.  The Board 
thinks new capacity to meet BYONC eligibility should be defined as capacity that has not yet 
cleared a Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) auction.  Additionally, the Board appreciates that the 
process for setting new capacity for the 2029/2030 BRA is underway.  To the extent new resources 
want to participate in the 2029/2030 BRA and serve as a BYONC resource, they should present 
PJM with a BYONC contract before the auction, as contemplated in Attachment DD-4 section 
VII(c), and commit to acting as a price taker – otherwise new resources clearing in the 2029/2030 
BRA should likewise not be eligible to serve as a BYONC resource.  
Principally, the Board does not think capacity resources that cleared for the first time in the 
BRAs for the 2027/2028, 2028/2029, and 2029/2030 (if they did not present a BYONC contract 
before the BRA, as noted above) DYs should qualify as BYONC because these resources have 
already been committed to contribute to our system’s reliability.  Frankly, these are not new 
resources that require additional price certainty to enter PJM’s uncertain investment environment, 
take on risks from federal regulatory uncertainty, and undergo longer project development 
timelines due to supply constraints and siting and permitting delays.  They are not resources that 
large loads brought to the system.  Rather, these are resources that have already committed to come 
 
13 See PJM IRAS Proposal, Attachments A and B.

7 
 
online in the next few DYs.  Our region is facing an enormous reliability shortfall, considering 
robust reforms to its wholesale markets, and has implemented and extended a lower maximum 
price cap through the BRA for the 2029/2030 DY, acknowledging that even the soaring capacity 
market clearing price cannot provide the certainty that developers need.  Thus, the BYONC and 
RBP serve an important role in attracting new supply investment that this provision undermines.   
Allowing already-cleared resources and resources that will newly clear in the 2029/2030 
BRA to serve as BYONC would allow New Large Load customers with the highest willingness to 
pay for firm capacity the ability to direct attractive terms and conditions toward resources that are 
already committed to coming online.  This will effectively result in New Large Loads being 
grandfathered into the RPM in the amount of the new MW UCAP between the 2027/2028 and 
2028/2029 DYs, which is 774.314 and 524.7 MW UCAP,15 respectively, of new generation and 
generation uprates.  These buyer-side bids should instead be directed to new supply resources that 
may be able to accelerate their time to commercial operation if they have more attractive bilateral 
and demand-side offers.  Moreover, this provision will allow new large-load data centers to 
sidestep their commitment in the Ratepayer Protection Pledge to “build, bring, or buy the new 
generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands,”16 as these 
BYONC commitments would be with supply resources that have already cleared the RPM to serve 
PJM’s broader customer base.   
 
14 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 2027/2028 Base Residual Auction Report 7 (2025) (“PJM 2027/2028 
BRA Report”), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2027-
2028/2027-2028-bra-report.pdf.  
15 PJM 2028/2029 BRA Report at 3. 
16 The White House, Ratepayer Protection Pledge (March 4, 2026) (“Ratepayer Protection Pledge”), 
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.

8 
 
The Board recognizes that, if new capacity were defined as new supply resources that have 
not yet cleared any RPM auction, it would result in gap between the beginning of IRAS service 
and the date by which new capacity procured through the next BRA would be expected to come 
online.  Specifically, IRAS eligibility begins June 1, 2027, while new capacity procured for the 
next BRA—for the 2029/2030 DY—would not be expected to come online until June 1, 2029.  
Therefore, New Large Loads that enter into arrangements with otherwise qualifying BYONC 
resources could remain subject to IRAS before those arrangements become effective,17 which may 
explain why PJM chose to include capacity resources that cleared an RPM auction for the first 
time in the BRAs for the 2027/2028, 2028/2029, and 2029/2030 DYs.  However, the Board thinks 
the inclusion of already-cleared resources departs from the core tenets that underpin this Proposal, 
including the Ratepayer Protection Pledge and the benefits of BYONC to the system at large.   
The Board thinks there are workable complementary protocols to recognize the benefits of 
New Large Loads in BYONC arrangements even when that capacity is not yet contributing power 
to the grid.  In fact, in its description of its planned IRAS filing, PJM staff recommended to EDCs 
and states that New Large Loads that do not have a BYONC arrangement may be subject to load 
reduction prior to load reduction of New Large Loads that have arranged for BYONC that has not 
yet achieved commercial operation.18  Such a tiered curtailment pathway could complement a 
 
17 There are several exceptions that could shorten this gap.  For example, new supply resources that clear 
in the RBP may have commercial operation dates earlier than 2029 and may not have previously cleared 
an RPM auction.  In that case, Eligible New Large Loads may have a portion of their capacity needs 
covered by Allocated RBP UCAP MWs as early as June 1, 2028.  Demand-side resources, including 
Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources, may also have shorter development 
timelines than new-build generation such as a gas combustion turbine or combined-cycle plant.  In 
addition, an Eligible New Large Load could satisfy some or all of its capacity needs through BYONC if 
an otherwise eligible resources clears the Third Incremental Auction (“IA”) for the 2027/2028 DY, 
scheduled for February 2027, or the Second or Third IAs for the 2028/2029 DY, scheduled for July 2027 
and February 2028, respectively.  
18 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., CIFP Framework for Service During Periods of Insufficient Resource 
Adequacy – PJM Proposal 3 (July 27, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-

9 
 
provision that requires new capacity to be capacity that has not yet cleared in any RPM auction, 
as New Large Loads with BYONC arrangements could still have a higher level of reliability than 
those without.   
 
Ultimately, there is no perfect solution.  New large loads are seeking to interconnect at a 
pace that supply resources are simply unable to keep up with, leaving PJM with a significant 
resource adequacy shortfall.  However, allowing capacity resources that have already been 
committed in the RPM to count toward BYONC will not contribute to resource adequacy and thus, 
the Board thinks this aspect of the proposed Tariff revisions should be severed. 
 
Limited Protest - IRAS and BYONC Obligations Should Not Expire After Three DYs Without a 
Shortfall 
The Board has concerns with PJM’s provision proposing that, upon three consecutive years 
with no capacity shortfall,19 IRAS "goes to sleep," relieving existing BYONC of their RPM 
participation obligations and rendering New Large Loads' BYONC obligations obsolete.20  PJM’s 
Proposal frequently refers to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge as a basis for having data centers 
“build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new 
energy demands” through a framework that includes IRAS, BYONC, and the exclusion of certain 
New Large Load amounts from the Variable Resource Requirement (“VRR”) Curve.21  However, 
 
are/public-disclosures/2026/20260727-cifp-framework-for-service-during-periods-of-insufficient-
resource-adequacy-executive-summary.pdf. To better align with the eligibility requirements in PJM’s 
IRAS proposal, “not yet achieved commercial operation” could be changed to “not cleared an RPM 
auction for that Delivery Year.”  
19 For purposes of these comments, the Board refers to a DY in which committed capacity, as determined 
after the Third IA, is less than the PJM Region Reliability Requirement as a DY in which PJM faces a 
“capacity shortfall.” 
20 PJM IRAS Proposal at 72. 
21 See Id. at 109.

10 
 
this exemption would relieve existing New Large Loads of the obligation to maintain their ten-
year new capacity commitments merely because PJM has not faced a capacity shortfall for three 
consecutive DYs.  
Furthermore, the Board is concerned about the provision in Attachment DD-4 section VIII(f) 
that existing BYONC capacity resources will be relieved of their RPM participation obligations 
should committed capacity equal or exceed the PJM Region Reliability Requirement for three 
consecutive DYs.22  In line with its other feedback, the Board does not think these obligations 
should be relieved merely because PJM does not face a capacity shortfall for three consecutive 
DYs.  The Board thinks New Large Loads should only continue to be reflected in the VRR Curve 
without corresponding BYONC obligations once their BYONC has completed the applicable 
requirements outlined in section VIII, including its ten-year RPM participation commitment, and 
has thereby demonstrated a meaningful and durable contribution to system reliability.  Because 
relieving BYONC of these obligations also eliminates certain resource-specific RPM participation 
requirements, this concern is heightened for DR and distributed energy resource (“DER”) Capacity 
Aggregation Resources, which would no longer be subject to the BYONC-specific requirement to 
participate as an Annual Demand Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource for the ten-
year period.  This framework could therefore result in a situation in which committed capacity 
equals or exceeds the PJM Region Reliability Requirement for three consecutive DYs, existing 
BYONC is relieved of its participation obligations, and the subsequent withdrawal of that capacity 
contributes to a renewed capacity shortfall.23   
 
22 Id. at Attachments A and B. 
23 The Board also notes that PJM IRAS Proposal Attachment DD-4, section VIII(f) does not expressly 
relieve the separate ten-year annual demonstration requirement for Demand Resources and DER Capacity 
Aggregation Resources in section VII(i)(ii), creating additional ambiguity regarding the obligations that 
remain after the three-year condition is met.

11 
 
Lastly, the Board thinks IRAS can continue to be a useful resource adequacy tool even in 
DYs in which PJM does not face a capacity shortfall and thus does not think the service should 
“go to sleep” or that Eligible New Large Loads should permanently lose that status once the system 
has sufficient capacity.  New Large Loads that have not secured sufficient capacity through 
BYONC arrangements or Allocated RBP UCAP MW should continue to be subject to differential 
reliability and, when system conditions require load reductions, should continue to be called on 
before Pre-Emergency Load Management Resources.  At a minimum, previously Eligible New 
Large Loads should again be subject to IRAS if PJM subsequently re-enters a capacity shortfall.  
The Board also requests clarification regarding the interaction between the three-year 
shortfall condition and PJM’s proposed exclusion of New Large Load amounts from the VRR 
Curve.  PJM states that, after three consecutive DYs without a capacity shortfall, all New Large 
Loads effectively become just “Large Loads,” and the in-service date cutoff for “New” Large Load 
resets prospectively once a capacity shortfall reemerges.24  At the same time, PJM indicates that 
New Large Load amounts without sufficient BYONC or Allocated RBP UCAP MW will remain 
excluded from the VRR Curve whether or not they are subject to IRAS, stating that securing 
sufficient capacity is the basis for subsequently reflecting such load in the VRR Curve.  Thus, the 
Board requests clarification that New Large Load amounts previously excluded from the VRR 
Curve will remain excluded notwithstanding the three-year condition unless and until the 
associated load secures sufficient capacity.   
 
Limited Protest - BYONC Arrangements Should Be Transferable 
 
24 PJM IRAS Proposal at 72.

12 
 
 
The Board thinks that BYONC should be transferable for New Large Loads and new supply 
resources.  PJM asserts that “[a]llowing BYONC to leave or be traded after entering into an 
arrangement with a New Large Load would dramatically increase the complexity of the program 
without commensurate benefit.”25  The Board disagrees.  Transferable BYONC obligations serve 
an important role.  Transferring BYONC can reduce long-term counterparty and performance risk 
and can allow a New Large Load to replace a resource that becomes uneconomic, unavailable, or 
otherwise unable to support the arrangement.  It can also allow a large load to transfer its BYONC 
to another large load if the two loads value reliable service differently from each other over time.  
The Board thinks there should be more flexibility for New Large Loads and new supply resources 
over the course of the ten-year BYONC term, and the Board suggests PJM and FERC sever this 
restrictive provision.   
 
The Board, however, thinks PJM provides a reasonable accommodation for Demand 
Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources.  These resources must show an initial ten-
year commitment, but they also have the ability to replace locations and contracts, if needed.  
However, the Board suggests that PJM’s proposed Tariff language provides further clarity on the 
eligibility of Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources that may qualify as 
BYONC, because as drafted, the criteria limits the eligibility of these resources to only those 
locations that have not participated in a prior RPM auction, which may be inappropriate if the 
characteristics of the load at such location have changed over time.  The Board requests that PJM 
allow more flexibility and permit a location to participate as a new Demand Resource or DER if 
the characteristics of the load have changed since it last participated in an RPM auction.  
 
 
25 Id. at 65.

13 
 
Limited Protest - PJMs Proposed IRAS Compensation Mechanisms Should Be Removed 
The Board thinks PJM’s compensation structure is ambiguous, unclear, and unnecessary, 
and requests that Attachment DD-4 section X, which puts forth the conditions of compensation for 
IRAS, is severed.  PJM states that whether a particular Eligible New Large Load is entitled to 
compensation will be determined by state authorities under state law.26  Attachment DD-4 section 
X establishes a wholesale rate of 50% of the Non-Performance Charge Rate unless the Eligible 
New Large Load elects to accept less compensation or waive it altogether.  The interaction between 
the rate, state action, and the large load is unclear.  For instance, if a state directs the large load to 
waive the rate through its retail tariff, is the large load obligated to waive it?  The Board is 
concerned that this mechanism may be setting up future litigation and disputes about who has the 
right to certain rate treatments.   
The Board thinks that the easier path is to sever the provision.  The compensation scheme 
appears intended, in part, to redress loads that may be subject to capacity price obligations even if 
they do not get the same reliability as other loads on the system.  However, if states wish to 
compensate Eligible New Large Loads for accepting reduced reliability of service in lieu of 
bringing their own capacity, they can do so through their existing retail ratemaking authority, and 
the large loads are fully able to challenge those retail ratemaking decisions through the proper 
venues.  Accordingly, the Board recommends that Attachment DD-4 section X of PJM’s proposed 
Tariff revisions be severed.  
III. 
Large Load Registry 
The Board supports the proposed Large Load Registry and appreciates PJM’s role in 
leading the development and maintenance of such registry.  The Large Load Registry will help 
 
26 Id. at 106.

14 
 
states and the relevant utilities develop standards and protocols for IRAS.  The Board appreciates 
PJM’s receptiveness in including this in its Proposal after encouragement from stakeholders during 
the CIFP process.  The Board will work with relevant state agencies, utilities, PJM, and large load 
customers, as needed, to ensure the Eligible New Large Loads in this registry are accurate and 
proper protocols are in place ahead of PJM curtailment directives.  
IV. 
Removal of Demand from VRR Curve 
The Board strongly supports PJM’s decision to remove uncovered incremental New Large 
Load amounts from the VRR Curve.  The Board has advocated for this in many stakeholder 
forums, including direct letters to the PJM Board of Managers from the Board’s President,27 and a 
separate letter from the Board’s Executive Director on this matter.28   
The Board has advocated this position for multiple reasons.  First, if Eligible New Large 
Loads29 subject to IRAS were included in the VRR Curve, the market would signal to these 
customers that the system will continue to procure capacity for them.  This would undermine one 
of the core tenets for designating this service to Eligible New Large Loads in the first place, which 
is to provide an incentive for these customers to procure their own capacity.  Additionally, keeping 
 
27 Letter from Christine Guhl-Sadovy, President, New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, to the PJM Board 
of Managers (Mar. 27, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-
disclosures/2026/20260401-njbpu-letter-re-connect-and-manage-issue-charge.pdf.  
28 Letter from Bob Brabston, Executive Director, New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, to the PJM Board 
(Nov. 18, 2025), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-
disclosures/2025/20251118-njbpu-staff-re-cifp-lla.pdf.  
29 “Eligible New Large Loads” is used here consistent with PJM’s definition of Eligible New Large Loads 
in its IRAS Proposal, i.e., “All New Large Loads shall be eligible to provide IRAS and considered 
Eligible New Large Loads to the extent the combination of their BYONC arrangements and Allocated 
RBP UCAP MW does not meet their capacity needs.” See proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section 
V(a); see also proposed Tariff, Definitions – Eligible New Large Load (‘“Eligible New Large Loads’ shall 
mean a New Large Load eligible to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service in accordance with 
Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section V.”); proposed Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section IV(a) (“All Eligible 
New Large Loads shall be available to be requested to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service by 
[PJM].”).

15 
 
loads subject to IRAS in the demand stack would cause existing ratepayers to pay to procure supply 
for these entities, as costs from the RPM are currently socialized across the region.  This would 
conflict with the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.30  Therefore, while the Board has some concerns 
with aspects of this section, it is an important step toward protecting ratepayers from high costs 
attributable to these customers.  Furthermore, removing these customers from the VRR Curve also 
protects ratepayers from the risks associated with uncertain New Large Load forecasts, 
appropriately placing this risk on the customers driving that growth rather than requiring existing 
ratepayers to procure capacity in advance for load that may not ultimately materialize.  This is 
particularly relevant as PJM predicts a summer peak load increase of nearly 100 GW over the next 
20 years.31  The Board commends PJM for making the removal of these loads a key component of 
its Proposal.     
However, to reiterate a previous request, the Board seeks clarification that Eligible New 
Large Loads will not be allowed into the VRR Curve so long as they have not fulfilled their 
capacity requirement through BYONC arrangements or Allocated RBP UCAP MW if the three-
year regional transmission organization (“RTO”) Reliability Requirement criterion is met.  
 
Limited Protest - The IRAS Trigger Must Account for Eligible New Large Load Amounts 
Importantly, PJM has not made it clear how the capacity shortfall will be determined after 
Eligible New Large Loads are removed from the VRR Curve.  Specifically, PJM has not clarified 
whether the PJM Region Reliability Requirement determined prior to the Third IA and used in 
section IV(b) is calculated before or after the deduction of the Excluded RTO New Large Load 
 
30 Ratepayer Protection Pledge (“Companies will build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and 
electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands, paying the full cost of those resources whether by 
building, or buying from, new or otherwise additive power plants.”). 
31 PJM 2026 Load Forecast Tables.

16 
 
Amounts.  The Board thinks the capacity shortfall determination should account for the Excluded 
RTO New Large Load Amounts used to reduce the VRR Curve.  This clarification is needed to 
better understand and evaluate other elements of PJM’s Proposal.  
 
Energy Market Costs Should Be Monitored  
To the extent that a significant amount of New Large Load elects to interconnect without 
BYONC or Allocated RBP UCAP MW, and thus remain subject to IRAS, energy prices may 
increase substantially for ratepayers.  We have yet to see how many New Large Loads will choose 
to be subject to IRAS service over seeking bilateral contract arrangements.  However, if a 
substantial amount of New Large Load fails to offset its registered peak load with sufficient 
capacity arrangements through BYONC or Allocated RBP UCAP MW and are subject to IRAS, 
PJM may need to consider additional measures to protect ratepayers from consistently higher costs 
in the energy market.  While there can be financial benefits to having a higher grid utilization rate 
at large, the Board suggests PJM and FERC monitor whether IRAS loads are resulting in 
substantially higher energy market costs.  In the future, it may be worth considering further 
incentivizing or requiring New Large Loads to bring commensurate new supply resources with 
them.  
V. 
Conclusion 
The Board commends PJM for proposing an RTO-led curtailment program that applies to 
New Large Loads that have not met their capacity obligations.  The Board also appreciates PJM’s 
proposed removal of Eligible New Large Loads from the VRR Curve, as it will protect ratepayers 
from many of the costs and risks associated with New Large Loads in the capacity market and 
better incentivize New Large Loads to bring their own new capacity.  However, the Board’s support 
does not come without concerns, and the Board requests that certain elements of the Proposal are

17 
 
severed where doing so would better uphold the Ratepayer Protection Pledge without significantly 
affecting the Proposal’s core components.  
 
Respectfully,
